One of the better games of its kind on Steam, and one I keep going back to because I haven't managed to get to the end in 8 hours. Honestly, it's pretty punishing and chaotic -- I'll chalk that up to my lack of skill rather than a lack of balance on the part of the game It certainly FEELS fun. Plus it has real slick pixel art style graphics and great music to go along with it. Never had a regret at this purchase, and I keep coming back to it after a break.

Steredenn is a game I really want to love, as while my total Steam playtime is low, my iOS playtime is well over a hundred hours. Unfortunately, I can’t recommend it to people because it’s a game that has all the right pieces for making something truly special, but it can’t quite figure out how to put those pieces together in order to achieve the promise of its full potential. 

It’s a game made by developers that obviously understand what type of game they enjoy, but somehow seems to lack an understanding of what makes a game of this kind genuinely [i]enjoyable[/i] to play. It’ll be adored by its audience, for sure, but it’ll never get the audience it deserves because its design speaks to the developers being profoundly adamant about it being what they want it to be, instead of even bothering to venture into what it has the potential to be.

I like this game. I don’t love it. And I can’t recommend it to other people as a result.

10 years after it originally release and it's still my favorite shmup! Every now and then I boot it up for a couple runs, especially now that we have steam decks.


Perfect blend of procedural generation to keep you on your toes but remaining predicable enough that you can learn all the waves and how to beat them flawlessly.

All the early bosses have multiple variants with their own unique patterns so it never feels too repetitive to die and start a new run over and over. And every time you meet a boss there's a funny line/pop culture reference to introduce them.

Lots of weapons and upgrades, granted not all of them are great but all of them are fun for sure!
A handful of player ships that each cater to a ceratin playstyle and have unique abilities.

Not enough? There's a handful of secret bosses that spice up your run with their own set of very powerful upgrades and usually increase the difficulty for every one of them you beat.

Beat the final boss? WRONG! There's another final final boss. Beat that one? Now you get to do it all over again but the enemies increase their volume of fire for every loop you go through.

Striking visuals that manage to still clearly convey to you what's going on on the screen (though it can get a bit hectic in the later stages especially if you're beyond the first loop)

And last but certainly not least, the banger of an OST, courtesy of Zander Noriega, that will make you feel like an absolute badass as you murder thousands of pirates across all of time and space.

If you like shmups, Steredenn is a must have and earns its place among the best of its kind.

Steredenn is an absolute gem of a game!

It's a sidescrolling space shoot-em-up roguelike, where you blast asteroids, enemy ships, and other stage hazards, before encountering progressively bigger and badder bosses. 

Each boss has alternate forms, with differing patterns of attack and unique weaknesses. The stages also vary in enemy composition and hazards. In each run you'll find different weaponry, of which you can hold 2 (as well as 1 ship-based equipment) and after each boss you get a choice of upgrades that you can use to create builds and synergies! There are hidden bosses, different ships to unlock, and it has an absolutely killer soundtrack! 

If you enjoy synergistic builds and looping mechanics, bullet hell, and the choice mechanics of other great games of the genre, you should definitely check it out! (And again, the soundtrack alone is outstanding!)

It is fast-paced, frantic, and very satisfying to beat! You can customize the settings to turn off screen shakes and bright flashes if you need. There are multiple game modes, boss rushes, coop, and tons of replayability through the various ship archetypes, upgrades, and weapon modules (you can build into heavy rocketry, lasers, melee weapons (?!), automated drones, and more!) 

So what are you waiting for?! There are space pirates and nasty infested asteroid monsters out there for you to blow up, chomp, and vaporize! Prepare for launch, and get ready to both perish in agony and kick ass, time and time again!

This is a game in which you pilot a grey and black spaceship. This spaceship exists in a dark black universe, where clusters of orange stars can be seen in the background. You being with your orange weapon shooting orange bullets at the enemy. Let me tell you something about the enemy. The first enemy came on screen, is this a friend? Is it a foe? You see, this spaceship was also black and orange, just like me. When the enemy spaceship shot its orange bullets at me I thought, for sure, this is the enemy. This must be destroyed. As I spray my orange bullets into its black and orange hull it exploded in an orange fiery death. Then, what is this? Another black and orange spaceship enters the screen, first one, then two. I assume this time they are the enemy and swiftly take them down. It's very important to be able to react to the orange bullet patterns of the enemies, so it's important to be able to distinguish which type of enemy it is as it enters the screen. So god bless the designers for making subtle differences to each enemy spaceship, for you see, these new enemies were a few pixels narrower and a few pixels less tall than my initially encountered enemies. But don't be deceived, black and orange spaceships are not your only enemy. No. There are black asteroids also, and... what is this that I see? A brown asteroid too. I was so confused and shocked, I began to question everything. I absorbed myself in the study of color for weeks before I could return to the game. What a fool I had been. A mere amateur of colour would think these meteors brown, but with my new aesthetic credentials I can assure you, that what novices call "brown" is more accurately referred to as "dark orange".

These orange bullets are not your only arsenal. Floating in space are small capsules, orange in color. I picked one up and was blessed with a majestic new weapon, entirely different to my prior gun. This time, large orange balls instead of small orange ellipses. I could barely contain my excitement at this radical new change.

When armed with sufficiently powerful orange projectiles you may be lucky enough to encounter a boss. Yes, these bosses will take you back. Orange and black ships, much larger than the orange and black ships you have encountered before. Be careful!

I have a few criticisms. The game only starts about one in every three times I attempt to launch it. I assume there were not enough orange and black pixels available on my monitor to fuel this game's ambitious needs. I suggest turning your OS wallpaper to white before attempting to start it.

Another criticism: one time the game clearly crashed because a power up capsule appeared that was neither brown nor black. An offensive blue. I dared pick it up and the my ship began spewing a ghastly blue laser. I promptly reset my own computer out of fear.

One other thing to note: it is possible to unlock a playable spaceship called the Red Baron. It may be called the *Red* Baron, but I assume it is orange and black.

I bought Steredenn after being lead to it by a Unity scripting tutorial kindly written by the developers. It's an arcade-style, side-scrolling bullet hell shooter more forgiving than old Gradius or Raiden games at the arcade by means of having a higher life count - yet also delightfully frustrating as the genre is often meant to be. The game is very fast-paced in terms of progression and enemy speed. Enemy bullets travel fast, but rocks and turrets take time to destroy. Controls are straightforward, controller-friendly, and remappable. It's helpful to see your hitbox (the green dots) at all times.

The tutorial ends in a surprising way integrating with the plot. The plot is quite straightforward too and there are a number of subplots with enjoyable archetypes to be discovered. There's humor in the subtitles. The sound effects are great, the original score is good too. The ships are well-defined and the backgrounds are breathtaking, though the backgrounds are drawn in a visibly finer resolution. Some will nitpick, but I'm glad the artists didn't attempt to fully replicate a 16-bit game for the sake of cheap nostalgia.

A major downside of the game is that the stages, bosses and weapons dropped are randomized each playthrough. For more hardcore players this may prevent score-counting from having any meaning. I have encountered one bug - sometimes when I try to enter the arena; all my buttons will stop functioning except for the back/escape button.

Despite the downsides I highly recommend this game. Its thematic coherence, relative ease at the beginning, and challenging learning curve are a suitable introduction for people new to the genre; as well as a joy for people who regularly play shoot-em-up games. It's frustrating but painfully addicting.

Steredenn mixes shoot 'em up with rogue-like and as a result, you get one of the most addicting, enjoyable and challenging game out there. 
You have 5 different ships that have very different play styles and each stage you get random weapons and upgrades that makes every run feel fresh and unique. It has awesome animations, great pixel art, tons of creative weapons, fun bosses, secrets and multiple game modes including co-op.
Though it is really challenging, none of it feels unfair. The indications and hit-boxes are really solid. 
It took me 25 hours to beat it a single time and still haven't conquered everything it offers.
I have nothing bad to say about it really. Steredenn is a must buy if you are a fan of either rogue-likes or shoot em ups.

I'm a big fan of Shmups like Ikaruga, Natsuki Chronicles, and Neko Navy.  None of them have captivated me as much as this game has.  I really enjoy navigating the upgrades/weapons options and find particular joy in making the drops work.

I have friends who don't love shmups as much but still enjoy this as a fun way to play cooperatively on something that requires little devotion to enjoy.
If you're looking for oldschool horizontal pixel schmups that has variety, is quick to get into, and you can quickly grow in, I think this is just the game for that.
